tldr: In reinforcement learning for legged locomotion, decomposing the effective rank of the policy Jacobian by gait phase (swing vs. stance) reveals representation health, enabling smooth sim-to-real transfer with roughly 3x lower joint jitter on a physical Spot robot.
hero_caption: Overall validation setup of this work. Large-scale training and analysis were performed in simulation (IsaacLab) on two quadrupeds and one humanoid (H1), followed by zero-shot transfer to a physical Boston Dynamics Spot.
overview:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has dramatically advanced agile locomotion skills in quadrupeds and humanoids. However, on-policy algorithms like PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) optimize non-stationary objectives, which easily causes neural networks to lose representational capacity (plasticity) as training progresses. In practice, practitioners mostly rely on reward curves during tuning, making it difficult to foresee from training-time signals whether a policy will move smoothly on hardware.

To address this, the authors introduced the effective rank of the policy Jacobian—which captures input-to-output sensitivity—as a metric to track representation health. Their key finding is that instead of looking at a global rank averaged across the entire gait cycle, one must evaluate rank conditioned on the gait phase: swing (foot in the air) versus stance (foot on the ground).

Experiments reveal that modern SimBa-style networks equipped with Layer Normalization and residual connections naturally allocate roughly two more dimensions of effective rank to swing than to stance, a trait completely absent in vanilla multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Applying a design recipe built around this architectural signature reduced unnecessary joint jitter by roughly 3x not only in simulation but also on a physical Boston Dynamics Spot, achieving highly accurate and smooth locomotion transfer.
contributions: Proposed a novel diagnostic approach to evaluate internal representation health during training via the effective rank of the policy Jacobian conditioned on gait phase (swing vs. stance).

Discovered that architectures with Layer Normalization and residual connections (SimBa) possess an inherent inductive bias that allocates roughly two more dimensions of rank to swing than stance, which is absent in vanilla MLPs.

Demonstrated that effective rank is not merely a metric to maximize, but acts as a health monitor capable of detecting representational breakdown under overfitting (rank inflation and phase-gap collapse).
Demonstrated smooth sim-to-real transfer on a physical Spot based on these findings, slashing joint jitter roughly threefold (high-frequency ratio dropped from 3.28% to 0.64%).

sections.heading: Why can't reward curves predict real-robot behavior?
sections.summary: While deep RL for legged locomotion is progressing rapidly, training reward curves alone cannot predict jitter or smoothness upon deployment on hardware. This section introduces a fresh perspective connecting representation health to hardware smoothness by evaluating the effective rank of the policy Jacobian conditioned on gait phases.
sections.details:
Combining massively parallel simulation with PPO has enabled quadrupeds and humanoids to perform acrobatic maneuvers such as parkour. Yet, the training process remains notoriously fragile. Non-stationary updates in PPO erode network plasticity—its ability to adapt to new tasks—making catastrophic forgetting more likely as curriculum stages advance.

To manage this, practitioners have empirically favored shallow MLPs, leaving the internal representations learned by these networks a black box. Although modern architectures incorporating Layer Normalization and residual connections (such as SimBa) have improved training stability and asymptotic performance, the underlying mechanism behind why their representations lead to superior physical behavior has remained unexplained.

This work examines the effective rank of the policy Jacobian, which captures input-output sensitivity. Because the Jacobian reflects how minute changes in observations affect actions, it is fundamentally tied to action smoothness in robot control. Furthermore, inspired by classical legged locomotion principles, the authors analyzed effective rank separately during the swing and stance phases of gait. This revealed critical architecture-specific representational signatures that global averaging across full cycles completely washes away.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of legged RL, representation collapse, and classical gait theory
sections.summary: This section organizes the three relevant contexts—sim-to-real challenges in legged RL, representation rank collapse inherent to RL, and classical gait phase theory—and explains how this study unifies them.
sections.details:
In deep RL for legged locomotion, policies trained purely on reward are well known to exhibit high-frequency action jitter that damages physical actuators. Traditional remedies have included tedious reward engineering on action rate-of-change, as well as imposing Lipschitz continuity constraints or Jacobian penalties directly on the policy network.

### PPO and Representational Non-Stationarity
Theoretical RL research points out that non-stationarity induced by policy updates causes a drop in the rank of feature representation matrices, leading to lost plasticity (rank deficiency). While PPO's clipping mechanism bounds drastic distribution shifts, it cannot prevent internal feature drift. Architectures with normalization blocks like SimBa were devised to counter these issues, but their detailed influence on robotic control has remained poorly understood.

### Integrating Classical Gait Principles
In robotics, gait has long been formulated as a geometric and temporal separation between swing and stance phases (such as Raibert's principles). This study bridges modern effective rank analysis in deep learning with this classical gait phase perspective, demystifying the black-box behavior of learned policies.

sections.heading: Network health check: the mathematics of effective rank and gait patterns
sections.summary: This section covers the reinforcement learning setup, the definition of effective rank, and the formulation for calculating the policy Jacobian effective rank measuring input-output sensitivity. It also outlines the mathematical background connecting these concepts to gait phases.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Reinforcement Learning Setup
The environment is formulated as a Markov Decision Process, optimizing a policy network $\pi_{\theta}$ and value network $\hat{v}_{w}$ using the PPO-Clip algorithm. The authors employ a standard pipeline (RSL-RL) featuring Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) and an adaptive learning rate controller conditioned on KL divergence.

### 3.2 Effective Rank Definition
To measure the dispersion of singular values in a matrix, the entropy effective rank ($\operatorname{erank}$) is utilized. Given singular values $\sigma_{i}$, numerically insignificant components are filtered out to form a normalized distribution $p_{i} = \sigma_{i} / \sum_{j}\sigma_{j}$. Its Shannon entropy is then evaluated as follows:
$$\operatorname{erank}(A) = \exp\left(-\sum_{i} p_{i} \ln p_{i}\right)$$
When the spectrum is uniform, rank is maximized; if biased toward a few dominant singular values, it approaches 1.

Beyond feature rank (penultimate representations) and weight rank (raw weight matrices), this work places central emphasis on the policy Jacobian effective rank ($r_{\mathrm{Jac}}$) to capture input-output sensitivity. For observation $x_{i}$, the gradient of the deterministic mean action $\pi_{\theta}(x_{i})$ is computed as $J_{\theta}(x_{i}) = \partial\pi_{\theta}(x_{i})/\partial x_{i}$, yielding the batch-averaged Jacobian $\bar{J}_{\theta}$. Crucially, the authors partition samples by phase index sets $\mathcal{I}_{p}$ (swing or stance) to compute the phase-conditioned rank $\operatorname{erank}(\bar{J}_{\theta,p})$ from $\bar{J}_{\theta,p}$.

### 3.3 Gait Patterns and Sensitivity Intuition
During a trot gait, four legs move according to low-dimensional coordination patterns. A healthy policy should maintain an appropriate dimensional sensitivity matching its active degrees of freedom, cleanly switching sensitivity dimensionality between swing (when legs move freely in the air) and stance (when supporting body weight). Verifying whether this dynamic shift occurs serves as the core diagnostic metric.

captions.F2: Conceptual diagram of the three rank metrics analyzed in this work: weight rank of weight matrices $W_{\ell}$, feature rank of penultimate representations $F_{\theta}(X)$, and effective rank of the policy Jacobian $J_{\theta}(x_{i})$ measuring local input-output sensitivity.

sections.heading: Experimental results: a 2-dimensional swing advantage and dramatic real-world smoothness
sections.summary: Through experiments in simulation and on a physical Spot, the authors discovered that SimBa architectures allocate roughly two more effective rank dimensions to swing than to stance. Policies exhibiting this signature achieve roughly 3x lower joint jitter on hardware. The authors also observed rank inflation and phase-gap collapse triggered by overfitting.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in IsaacLab using RSL-RL, comparing standard MLPs against SimBa variants with Pre-LN residual connections. Evaluations were performed on a physical Boston Dynamics Spot, as well as ANYmal-D (quadruped) and Unitree H1 (19-DoF humanoid) in simulation.

### Phase Conditioning Reveals the "Swing Advantage"
Analyzing the post-training Jacobian effective rank revealed that SimBa consistently allocated roughly two more dimensions of effective rank to swing than to stance ($\Delta_{\phi} = \operatorname{erank}(J_{\mathrm{swing}}) - \operatorname{erank}(J_{\mathrm{stance}}) \approx +2.14$). In contrast, vanilla MLPs lacked this separation entirely, even showing a slightly negative delta ($-0.31$).
Crucially, looking at global Jacobian effective rank averaged across the full gait cycle yields virtually identical numbers: 9.3 for SimBa and 9.2 for MLP, completely masking this vital structural difference. Phase conditioning is what finally makes this fundamental architectural inductive bias visible.

### Hardware Transfer to Spot and Remarkable Smoothness
This representation health translated directly into physical performance. Both in simulation and on the physical Spot, SimBa policies drastically slashed joint jitter (high-frequency ratio HFR) by roughly 3x compared to MLPs (from 3.28% in MLP-XXL down to 0.64% in SimBa-XXL). Furthermore, base velocity tracking RMSE improved by 62.7% (from 0.176 m/s to 0.066 m/s), resulting in highly smooth locomotion without foot chattering.

### "Higher Rank Isn't Always Better": The Overfitting Trap
Intentionally inducing overfitting (representation collapse) by doubling PPO update epochs uncovered striking behavior. In overfitted SimBa policies, feature rank inflated abnormally (+66%), and Jacobian rank saturated near its upper bound. Consequently, the healthy swing-dominant phase gap ($\Delta_{\phi}$) collapsed toward zero. Notably, task reward and simulated tracking performance barely degraded during this collapse, creating an illusion of success. This demonstrates that effective rank is not a raw metric to maximize, but a diagnostic monitor for tracking representation health.

captions.F3: Comparison of Jacobian effective rank decomposed by gait phase. (a) SimBa shows a consistent positive phase gap across all settings with swing exceeding stance ($\Delta_{\phi} \approx +2.14$), whereas MLP remains at or below zero. (b) Averaged globally, both sit around 9.2–9.3, demonstrating why phase conditioning is essential.
captions.F6: Sim-to-real transfer results on physical Spot and other robots. In both (a) joint control jitter (HFR %) and (b) velocity tracking RMSE, SimBa transfers reliably from simulation (light) to hardware (dark), preventing the severe degradation and jitter observed in MLP. (c) Similar low-jitter trends are confirmed on ANYmal-D and H1 (humanoid).
captions.F7: Process of representation breakdown caused by overfitting. (a) Overfitting drives abnormal inflation in feature rank (+66%). (b) As a result, the phase gap $\Delta_{\phi}$ signifying healthy learning collapses toward zero. (c) Standard gait reward fails to detect this collapse, highlighting the danger of relying solely on rewards.

sections.heading: Recognized limitations and future challenges
sections.summary: The authors identify several limitations, including the primary focus on blind flat-terrain locomotion, the need to examine diverse architectures like Transformers, and exploring asymmetric Actor-Critic configurations.
sections.details:
While validated on a physical Spot robot, the authors acknowledge several limitations:

- Experiments primarily targeted blind flat-terrain locomotion. How this phase-gap signature behaves in rough terrain or when integrated with rich exteroception (vision and LiDAR) remains to be fully explored.
- Architectural comparisons focused primarily on SimBa versus MLP, leaving recurrent models (LSTM), Transformers, and alternative normalization techniques unexamined.
- Investigating how Jacobian effective rank is influenced by decoupled Actor-Critic trunks or asymmetric capacity designs—an emerging trend in robotic learning—is left for future research.

sections.heading: Conclusion: rethinking robot control through representation health
sections.summary: Gait-phase-conditioned policy Jacobian effective rank provides a powerful diagnostic tool for RL locomotion policies. Closely correlated with hardware smoothness during transfer, mechanistic analysis opens new paths toward improving the reliability of robot learning.
sections.details:
This paper establishes an approach to evaluate policy Jacobian effective rank conditioned on gait phases (swing vs. stance) during PPO training for legged robots. Global phase averaging masks crucial architectural differences, whereas phase conditioning highlights SimBa's ~2-dimensional swing advantage, directly linking it to a threefold reduction in hardware joint jitter.

Furthermore, the finding that overfitting inflates rank while destroying phase separation provides a key takeaway: effective rank is a health monitor, not an optimization objective to maximize. Moving beyond naive reward chasing, this work opens up a mechanistic perspective on internal representations to guarantee physical control quality.

sections.heading: Appendix: SimBa implementation details and the Spot hardware recipe
sections.summary: This section covers architectural implementation details such as depth-dependent residual scaling, as well as contact state estimation and the inference pipeline on physical Spot.
sections.details:
### SimBa Implementation Details (Appendix A.1)
To prevent gradient explosion across depth $N$, the SimBa block introduces a residual scaling factor $\alpha = 1/\sqrt{N}$ (original SimBa uses $\alpha=1$). In addition, empirical observation normalization tracking running statistics is applied to handle scale discrepancies across input channels.

### Spot Hardware Deployment (Appendix C.1)
The physical Spot lacks binary foot contact sensors. Leveraging the physical relationship where knee torque $\tau_{\text{knee}}$ is directly proportional to vertical ground reaction force $F_{z}$ via the leg Jacobian, accurate contact estimation (swing vs. stance) is performed via knee torque thresholding. Policy inference runs via ONNX Runtime on an external PC (Intel i7) at 50 Hz with 2–5 ms latency, communicating with the Spot SDK via gRPC.

takeaways: Jacobian effective rank in locomotion policies misses fundamental structural patterns unless evaluated separately for swing and stance.
LayerNorm combined with residual connections (SimBa) provides an inductive bias allocating roughly 2 more rank dimensions to swing, translating directly to low-jitter hardware motion.
Effective rank should be treated as a diagnostic health signal to catch overfitting and representational collapse, rather than an objective to maximize.
Internal representations can collapse (phase gap disappearing) even while reward curves keep improving, offering an early warning for sim-to-real transfer failure.
limitations: Evaluations focused primarily on blind locomotion on flat terrain; generalization to rough terrain with active exteroception (vision/LiDAR) requires future study.
Comparisons were limited to SimBa and MLP, leaving sequence models like Transformers and RNNs unexamined.
While a strong co-occurrence was shown between the phase rank gap and hardware smoothness, a formal mathematical model establishing strict causality remains to be constructed.
